A proposition is something that is put forward — an idea, a statement, an offer, or a plan that is placed in front of someone for them to consider, accept, reject, or respond to. Think of it as anything someone "puts on the table."

The word has several distinct meanings depending on the context, and understanding all of them will give you complete command of this word.
Meaning 1: A Statement That Can Be True or False

In logic, philosophy, and academic thinking, a proposition is a clear, definite statement that declares something to be true or false. It is not a question, not a command, not a wish — it is a claim about reality.

  • "The Earth is round" is a proposition. It makes a claim that is either true or false.
  • "All humans are mortal" is a proposition.
  • "Please close the door" is NOT a proposition — it's a command.
  • "Is it raining?" is NOT a proposition — it's a question.

A proposition has to be the kind of statement you can point at and say, "Is this true or false?" If you can do that, it's a proposition.

In mathematics, propositions are statements that can be proven, like: "The sum of two even numbers is always even."

In everyday life and business, a proposition is simply a proposal — an offer or suggestion put forward for someone to consider. This is the most common meaning in ordinary conversation.

  • A company might offer you a business proposition — a deal or plan they want you to agree to.
  • "He came to me with an interesting proposition: I would design the website, and he would handle the marketing."

Here, the proposition is essentially saying: "Here is my offer. What do you think?" It is an invitation to negotiate, agree, or decline.

A value proposition is a popular business term — it means the specific benefit or value a company promises to give its customers. It answers the question: "Why should you choose us?"
Meaning 3: A Task, Situation, or Person Being Considered

In informal usage, "proposition" can describe how difficult, complex, or risky a particular task, situation, or person is. This is used when you want to characterize something in terms of what it demands from you.

  • "Climbing Mount Everest is no easy proposition." → It's a very demanding undertaking.
  • "Dealing with him is a tough proposition." → He is a difficult person to deal with.
  • "Starting a business in this economy is a risky proposition." → It involves considerable risk.

Think of it as saying: "When you consider what this involves, here's what kind of thing it is."
Meaning 4: A Ballot Measure (Politics/Law, especially in the US)

In American politics, a proposition is a specific question or measure put to the public to vote on, usually appearing on a ballot by number.

  • "Proposition 13 changed how property taxes were calculated in California."

Here, a proposition is literally something "put forward" to the voters — they decide whether to approve or reject it.

In informal usage, to receive a proposition can also mean to receive an unsolicited or forward romantic or sexual offer from someone. While this meaning is less formal, it is well-established in everyday language.

  • "She was propositioned by a stranger at the bar." (Here it's used as a verb, but the noun form works the same way: "She received an unwanted proposition.")

Even though these meanings seem different on the surface, they all share the same underlying idea: something is placed in front of you and you must engage with it — by believing it or not, accepting it or not, voting on it or not, or dealing with it.

ContextWhat's being "put forward"
  • In logic → a statement put forward to be judged as true or false
  • In business/life → an offer put forward to be accepted or rejected
  • In everyday speech → a situation or task put forward as something to be dealt with
  • In politics → a measure put forward to be voted on
  • In informal social life → an advance put forward to be welcomed or refused

"A tough proposition" — something or someone that is hard to handle or deal with.

"A risky proposition" — something that involves significant risk.

"A business proposition" — a formal offer or deal in a commercial context.

"A value proposition" — the promise of benefit a product or service makes to a customer.

"An attractive proposition" — something that seems appealing and worth considering.

"Prove a proposition" — to demonstrate logically or mathematically that a statement is true.
The Subtle Difference Between "Proposition" and Similar Words

• A proposition is broader and more formal than a suggestion — it implies something more structured, more serious, or more defined.
  • A proposition is not quite the same as a question — a question asks; a proposition declares or offers.
  • A proposition differs from a fact — a fact is already accepted as true; a proposition is something still being put forward for consideration.

If you ever forget what "proposition" means, remember this simple phrase:

"Something put on the table for you to deal with."

Whether it's a logical statement, a business deal, a ballot measure, or a challenge — all meanings of proposition come back to that single image: something placed before you, waiting for your response.
